planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall; avoid planting during peak summer heat to let roots establish.

directions: Site in full sun for the brightest chartreuse color or part shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch. Space plants 4-6 feet apart to allow the upright, arching habit to fill out without crowding. Prune hard in early spring before new growth emerges, since flowers and fall color appear on new wood. Mulch to retain even soil moisture, especially through the first two seasons.

planting.note: Install balled-and-burlapped or container plants in spring or fall; water deeply at planting to settle soil around the root ball.

directions: Plant where tiered, horizontal branching can be viewed from above or below, such as a slope or stepped bed. Part shade helps preserve the clear white bloom color and reduces stress in warmer zones within its range. Prune immediately after the April flower show if shaping is needed, since buds for next year's bloom form on the current season's growth. Give it room to spread fully rather than crowding it against walls or other shrubs.

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall; in zone 6 provide winter wind protection the first couple seasons.

directions: Place near a path or patio where the fragrant May flower lace can be appreciated up close. In mild winters the leathery dark green foliage persists, so part shade and a wind-sheltered spot help it stay evergreen. Water regularly during the first growing season to establish the compact, rounded form. Prune only lightly right after bloom to maintain its naturally tidy shape.

planting.note: Set out container plants after the soil has warmed in spring, or in early fall with enough time to root in before frost.

directions: Use as a low edging or foundation shrub where the white-margined foliage and red-purple new stems add contrast through three seasons. Tolerates light shade well, though more sun deepens the pink fall leaf-margin color. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering, making it a good low-water border choice. Trim lightly in late winter only to remove dead wood, since it blooms on new growth from early summer into fall.

planting.note: Plant in a spot with reliably moist soil; this Netherlands-bred selection tolerates damp or boggy ground better than drier sites.

directions: Site along a rain garden edge or low spot where soil stays consistently damp, since this dogwood is bred to handle wet feet. Part shade keeps the purple-and-gray foliage from bleaching in hot afternoon sun while still allowing strong red winter stem color to develop. Cut one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each spring to keep producing vivid young wood, since winter color is best on new growth. Allow the full 5-7 foot spread for hedging or screening rather than pruning it into a tight shape.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall; this tough native selection establishes quickly in average to damp garden soil.

directions: Use on a shaded slope or woodland edge where the chartreuse-to-apricot foliage brightens dim corners through summer. It is unusually tolerant of both drought and periodically wet soil, making it forgiving in difficult sites. Deadheading spent flowers encourages the June-to-fall rebloom cycle that draws pollinators. A light shaping prune in early spring keeps the upright, spreading habit tidy without sacrificing the summer flower show.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall; adaptable to both drought and periodically wet soils once established.

directions: Tuck into a small-space or front-of-border planting where the near-black foliage can contrast against lighter companions in part shade. The compact 3-foot size fits tight urban lots and container groupings better than larger native honeysuckles. Yellow flowers rebloom through the season, so leave spent blooms in place rather than deadheading aggressively if seed interest is wanted for birds. Cut back lightly in early spring to refresh the dark foliage color for the new season.

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall in soil that holds moisture well; performs especially well in rain gardens and damp low spots.

directions: Plant where damp soil or periodic standing water would stress other shrubs, since this dogwood is bred to thrive in rain gardens. Part shade keeps the chartreuse summer foliage from scorching while the glossy scarlet winter stems still color up well. Coppice one-third of older stems to the ground each early spring to maximize the vivid red bark display next winter. Give it the full 4-6 foot spread in a mounded border rather than crowding it, since dense planting hides the winter stem color.
